title: NVHBM: Can Custom HBM Change Who Builds the Memory Stack?
gist: Per Oct 18 Seoul Economic Daily reporting, NVIDIA asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to build NVHBM logic base dies (integrating NVIDIA's custom memory controller) on TSMC 3 nm and standardize DRAM on the 1c generation. The author argues this could modularize HBM manufacturing across system designer, foundry, memory maker and packager, but a standardized design does not create manufacturing equivalence — stacking yield, test, thermal and qualification remain the real tests.

insights.claim: According to October 18, 2026 Seoul Economic Daily reporting, NVIDIA asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to use TSMC's 3 nm process for NVHBM logic base dies and to standardize DRAM dies on the sixth-generation 1c process.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Points to more TSMC advanced-node demand from HBM base dies and greater NVIDIA control over memory specs; treat as unconfirmed reporting.
insights.locator: According to October 18 reporting from Seoul Economic Daily

insights.claim: Samsung reportedly accepted NVIDIA's requirement to use TSMC for NVHBM base dies despite traditionally relying on its own foundry for HBM production, though this is industry reporting rather than a confirmed agreement.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: A negative signal for Samsung Foundry's captive HBM base-die business and a positive one for TSMC.

insights.claim: NVHBM moves NVIDIA's custom memory controller from the accelerator into the HBM base die, making the base die a more significant architectural component and enabling its fabrication to be separated from specialized DRAM processes.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Shifts value in the HBM stack toward logic base dies and the foundry that makes them.

insights.claim: NVHBM extends an existing trend: SK hynix partnered with TSMC on HBM4 base dies in April 2024, and Marvell introduced a custom HBM architecture with base-die logic and controller functionality in December 2024; NVIDIA's twist is a common custom architecture across multiple memory suppliers.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Custom HBM is becoming the norm for AI accelerators, increasing foundry content per HBM stack.
insights.locator: In April 2024, SK hynix announced a collaboration

insights.claim: A standardized custom HBM base die could split responsibilities among the system designer (controller and interface), a logic foundry (base die), the memory maker (DRAM and stacking) and an advanced packaging provider (integration with the accelerator).
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Useful map for where value and margin could migrate in the HBM chain.

insights.claim: A common HBM architecture does not create interchangeable memory stacks: suppliers on the same base-die process and DRAM generation can still differ in operating margins, thermal behavior, power, variation and reliability.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Memory makers keep differentiation and pricing power even under NVIDIA standardization — don't assume HBM commoditizes.
insights.quote: A standardized design creates the possibility of modular manufacturing. It does not establish manufacturing equivalence.
insights.locator: A common architecture does not automatically

insights.claim: Splitting HBM manufacturing across organizations makes integration boundaries more critical — base-die-to-DRAM interfacing, TSV and bonding yield, shifted power dissipation from the controller, and cross-company failure isolation and traceability.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Watch for yield and qualification delays in multi-vendor custom HBM programs.
insights.quote: A qualified base die and individually tested DRAM dies do not guarantee a high-yield completed stack.
insights.locator: 3. Where Do the Manufacturing Challenges Move?

insights.claim: Modular HBM manufacturing only pays off if specialization benefits outweigh added logistics, intermediate testing, traceability, yield-ownership and coordination costs.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Limits how far disaggregation of HBM production can go economically.

insights.claim: Existing HBM makers would retain significant differentiation through DRAM cell density, power efficiency, stacking capability, process control and yield even if base-die manufacturing moves to a logic foundry.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Incumbent memory makers' moats are in DRAM and stacking, not base-die logic — new entrants face a high bar.
insights.locator: Existing HBM manufacturers would also retain

insights.claim: A new entrant to HBM supply would still need competitive DRAM technology, qualified stacking and bonding, known-good-die strategies, thermal characterization, failure analysis and product qualification; a foundry/assembler-led HBM model is a possible future, not an established consequence of NVIDIA's requirements.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Temper narratives that NVHBM opens HBM to new suppliers soon.
insights.locator: A company entering this supply chain

insights.claim: The real proof that modular HBM works is not announcing a shared base-die process but multiple suppliers repeatedly delivering complete stacks that meet common qualified requirements under varying temperature, voltage, workload and aging.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Track qualification outcomes across Samsung, SK hynix and Micron for NVHBM as the key milestone.
insights.quote: Standardizing the design does not standardize the product.
insights.locator: 5. What Would Prove That the Model Works?

insights.claim: NVHBM illustrates a broader semiconductor trend where architectural ownership and manufacturing ownership no longer need to reside in the same company, increasing the importance of interface definitions, test coverage, traceability and qualification.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: System designers like NVIDIA gain leverage over component specs, shifting bargaining power in the memory chain.
